source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Founding transfer paradigm. People read a military story (fortress taken by converging small forces), then solve Duncker's radiation problem. With an explicit hint, most use the analogy. Without a hint, few do.
numbers: Appropriate analog with hint: about 75% gave the convergence solution; control under 10%. Memorised story with no hint: about 30%. Authors infer only a third or less of those able to use the analogy noticed it unaided.
quote: only about 30% of our subjects produced the convergence solution, as opposed to about 75% who produced it when a hint was given
limits: Summary section of the 1983 paper, pooling the earlier 1980 studies; student samples; one ill-defined problem.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for O7: the bottleneck is noticing the source, not applying it. A scaffold must trigger or supply the source itself.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer Exp 1 (cord problem)
finding: Replicated the effect with Maier's two-cord problem and a different story. Analog helped before and after the hint. Summarising the story instead of recalling it made no real difference.
numbers: Before hint: analog groups 71% vs control 20% (G2(1)=15.8, p<.001). Total: 98% vs 30% (G2(1)=30.1). Recall 68% vs summary 75% after hint comparison n.s. Ns 20 to 25 per cell.
limits: High school classes, booklet format. Pendulum solution is easier to see than the radiation one.
agent_relevance: Transfer is not specific to one puzzle. The high no-hint rate here shows an easy, near target; difficulty of noticing depends on how close source and target are.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer Exp 2 (stating the principle)
finding: Adding an explicit statement of the convergence principle to the story did not help transfer. Principle alone also did about as well as the story.
numbers: Before hint: analog plus principle 32% (n=31), analog only 29% (n=28), principle only 28% (n=29). Totals 80%, 79%, 66%; differences n.s., G2(2)=2.05, p=.36.
limits: Null result, small cells; principle-only group was not far behind.
agent_relevance: Telling the model an abstract rule did not beat showing a worked analog here. Do not assume a stated principle replaces an example, or the reverse; test both.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer Exp 3 (diagrams)
finding: A diagram of converging arrows added to the story did not raise spontaneous transfer. Diagram alone, without a story, rarely produced the solution unprompted.
numbers: Total solutions about 80% for both story conditions. Diagram-only: 1 of 15 subjects (7%) solved before the hint; total 67% vs 78% for analog conditions.
limits: Small cells. The convergence solution was almost never spontaneous without the story.
agent_relevance: A richer surface format does not fix retrieval. Schema must be induced from content.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer Exp 4 (two analogs vs one)
finding: Comparing two stories with the same principle helps people induce a schema and transfer it. Similar and dissimilar pairs worked about equally. Schema quality predicted transfer strongly.
numbers: Unprompted solutions: two analogs 45% vs one analog plus control 21% (G2(1)=6.35, p<.01). Totals 80% vs 53% (G2(1)=8.36). Similar pair 39%, dissimilar pair 52% (n.s.). Schema quality: 21% good, 20% intermediate, 59% poor; 91% of good-schema subjects solved with no hint (G2(4)=15.8, p<.005).
limits: Schema quality was scored from subject written descriptions, so it is correlational. Cell sizes small (n 23 to 47).
agent_relevance: Strongest basis for an O7 design: use two or more sources and make the agent write the common principle, then solve from the principle. Check the written schema.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus & Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: Algorithm and Examples
finding: Computational form of Gentner's structure-mapping theory. A mapping M pairs base items with target items, one-to-one, and must be structurally consistent: if two relations are paired, their arguments are paired too. Object attributes are dropped. Relations tied into higher-order systems are kept over isolated ones (systematicity).
numbers: Worked example: water flow to heat flow. Pressure relation under CAUSE maps to temperature relation; the isolated relation GREATER-THAN(DIAMETER(beaker),DIAMETER(vial)) is discarded.
quote: it is the amount of common higher-order relational structure that determines which of several possible matches is preferred
limits: Hand-built symbolic descriptions are given as input. The engine does not find the representations.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable definition of a good mapping: one-to-one, argument-consistent, scored by depth of shared relational structure. Fits our rule that code, not the model, checks the mapping.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus & Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: Algorithm and Examples (complexity)
finding: SME builds local matches, merges them into global mappings (gmaps) without backtracking, scores them, and then makes candidate inferences. Most steps are linear or low polynomial. The final merge step is factorial in the worst case.
numbers: Stated as O(N) for most steps; last critical merge step O(N!) worst case; authors report typical cases far better.
limits: Complexity claims are from the authors' own analysis and runs on small to medium descriptions.
agent_relevance: A mapping check on a few dozen facts is cheap in code. Keep typed mappings small so the check stays tractable.

source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science 7
finding: Proposes that analogy maps relations, not attributes, and prefers systems of interconnected relations. The fetched copy is a scan with mostly garbled text, so only the systematicity and relations-not-attributes statements were confirmed in it.
numbers: No experimental numbers read from this scan.
limits: OCR of the scan was mostly garbled. Details here rely on the SME paper and the 2023 LLM papers that apply the theory.
agent_relevance: Basis for scoring a mapping by relational structure and not by surface overlap (see ARN results below).

source: Hodel & West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Replication with changes. Changing the alphabet or letter interval in letter-string problems collapses GPT-3 on most problem types. Humans stay stable. Authors argue the Webb zero-shot claim cannot rule out training contamination.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy on synthetic alphabet below 0.1 for extend sequence, successor/predecessor and fix alphabetic sequence. Only remove-redundant and sort stayed near original level. N=50 instances per condition for GPT-3.
limits: text-davinci-003 only. Comprehension checks showed GPT-3 could process the modified alphabets (at least 30% of original level on all but one check).
agent_relevance: A pattern that works on standard material may be recall. Test O7 on altered or counterfactual versions before trusting it.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Systematic counterfactual test of the Webb letter-string result. Permuted alphabets and symbol alphabets drop all three GPT models and not humans. The models also answered simple comprehension checks about the new alphabets, so the failure is not mere misunderstanding.
numbers: Overall accuracy across all alphabets: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1,876 samples, 136 Prolific participants); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each; the table lists them in the order GPT-3, 3.5, 4). 420 problems per permutation level n=2,5,10,20; 40 symbol problems.
limits: Zero-generalization problems only. Chat models may be worse at this task than base models. Human accuracy was higher than in Webb's sample.
agent_relevance: Reported human-level analogy in LLMs is brittle. An agent should check an analogy by running it on a changed instance (guardrail G3).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (error types)
finding: Error mix differs by model. GPT-3.5 often applied an alternate rule on counterfactual items, a sign of using a familiar rule instead of the one shown.
numbers: Alternate-rule errors: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22.00%, GPT-3.5 38.59% (as ordered in the table; humans around 15% in a related category).
limits: Error coding done by the authors on a sample; column-to-model order read from a flattened table.
agent_relevance: Failure is often a swap to a familiar rule. A code check against the stated rule on the new instance would catch this.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour (matrices)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text Digit Matrices built on Raven-like rules. Its error pattern followed human difficulty effects: progression rules harder, more distinct rules harder, misaligned logic problems harder.
numbers: Humans N=40. GPT-3 above humans on generative answers and on multiple choice (OR 6.27, p=2.3e-8, CI 3.28 to 11.99). Item-type correlation with humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: Text-only digit format, no pixel parsing. Prompt order effects. Possible training-data exposure of materials.
agent_relevance: Relational rule induction in text is within reach. Supports O6 re-description of a problem into a clean symbolic form before solving.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour (letter strings)
finding: GPT-3 solved novel letter-string analogies, including with generalisation from source to target, at or above human level on most types.
numbers: Humans N=57 UCLA undergraduates; 100 problems per type for GPT-3. Exact per-type values were only in figures that did not extract.
limits: Later counterfactual replications (Hodel and West; Lewis and Mitchell) show collapse under altered alphabets.
agent_relevance: Do not cite this as evidence of general mapping without the counterfactual caveats.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour (verbal analogies)
finding: On four-term verbal analogies GPT-3 matched or beat humans on UCLA-VAT and Sternberg-Nigro sets, beat the estimated high-school SAT average on 374 Turney SAT items, and was numerically weaker on the Jones set. It showed the human distance effect (semantically far A:B vs C:D harder).
numbers: Humans N=57 (UCLA VAT) and N=241 (Jones et al.). SAT set 374 items, 5 choices. Semantic distance effect in GPT-3: OR=3.24, p=0.0165, CI [1.24, 8.5].
limits: SAT and some sets were likely in web training data. Authors flag this.
agent_relevance: Word-pair analogy is a strength, probably partly memorised. Do not extrapolate to far-domain transfer.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour (story analogies)
finding: On Gentner et al. story pairs GPT-3 preferred the target sharing causal relations. It was clearly weaker than college students on this task. Preliminary GPT-4 was better.
numbers: Humans N=54; humans vs GPT-3 main effect OR=0.37, p=0.0003; GPT-3 binomial test p=0.0039 in one condition; 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story on every trial.
limits: Small item set from earlier human studies. GPT-3 has no long-term memory so cannot retrieve past episodes as a source.
agent_relevance: The hard case for our O7 is far, cross-domain, causal-structure matching, the exact case where distant sources are meant to help.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Benchmark built on Gentner's surface vs relational vs system mappings in narratives. Models do ok on near analogies and fail on far ones, and fail when a surface-similar distractor competes with a far true analogy.
numbers: Humans 96% overall vs models 57% (distinguishing analogies from distractors). Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% (below the 50% chance baseline). Best model GPT-4 68.1% average, SBERT 42.3%. Far analogy vs near distractor: models 33.9%. (far,far) 45.3%; (near,far) 76.9%; (near,near) 73.2%.
limits: Multiple choice with 50% baseline. Zero-shot prompts; instructions to prefer system mappings did not fix the near-distractor failure.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity captures LLMs. Retrieval of sources by embedding similarity will mislead; a mapping must be verified by relational structure in code.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning. J. Memory and Language 145
finding: New tasks that map semantic words to symbol sequences. Best LLMs (GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama-405B) match humans in default conditions, but differ when structure is generalised or when random words distract. Humans can ignore useless words, models are pulled by them.
numbers: 194 Brown students (132 and 62 across two experiments). Humans matched reference in 0.4 to 0.9 of answers; best LLMs 0.1 to 0.95 across conditions. Distracted condition dropped about 0.25 for humans and models alike. Models and humans both improved across successive questions.
limits: Authors conclude LLMs offer a how-possibly, not how-actually, account of human analogy. Many weaker models performed poorly.
agent_relevance: Model analogy is sensitive to distracting lexical content. Present the source in stripped, structural form when mapping.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis & Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Encoding Raven's matrices (RAVEN) into language with entity names, then decomposing into components and attributes, lifts zero-shot accuracy to human level and beyond on some sub-tasks. Higher abstraction helps small models most.
numbers: GPT-3 175B naming alone 77.2% on Center sub-task. With decomposition: 77.6% L-R, 78.0% U-D, 82.8% O-IC, 92.6% O-IG (exceeding humans on the latter). OPT 1.3B improved from 20 to 30% to over 70%.
limits: Hand-written encoding of perceptual attributes; the model does not see pixels. Noise attribute orientation excluded then tested separately.
agent_relevance: Strong support for O6: the same model gains about 20 points or more when the problem is re-expressed in structured terms. Also shows that representation, not the mapping step, carries much of the gain.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR (GSM8K, MATH)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant example problems and then solves the target. Beats 0-shot CoT, matches or beats manual few-shot CoT, with no labelled examples.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. MATH PaLM2: 27.1, 29.8, 34.3, 34.8. GSM8K text-davinci-003: 14.8, 50.3, 54.0, 61.0.
limits: Gain over few-shot CoT on GSM8K is about 1 point for GPT-3.5, probably within noise. Table rows were read in order from a flattened extraction; alignment is inferred.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogs help a little on known domains. This is the cheap form of O7; the gain is small where the model already knows the type.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR (Codeforces, BIG-Bench)
finding: On hard code problems, asking the model to first write core knowledge and then examples gives the biggest lift. Knowledge steered the examples to the same algorithm rather than a lookalike.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-3.5-16k: 0-shot 8%, 0-shot CoT 9%, 3-shot CoT 11%, self exemplars 13%, knowledge plus exemplars 15% (GPT-4: 16, 16, 17, 17, 19). Acc@10 GPT-3.5: 24, 27, 27, 25, 29. BIG-Bench temporal sequences: 40.4 (0-shot CoT) up to 58.0 with self exemplars; logical deduction 5 objects 30.0 to 41.6.
limits: Small test sets. Wins vary by task; formal fallacies gain was 2 to 3 points. Row alignment in tables inferred.
agent_relevance: The knowledge-then-example order is a usable O7 step: name the principle first, then pick analogs. Matches the schema-induction finding from Gick and Holyoak.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR (scale, generation vs retrieval)
finding: Self-generated exemplars need a strong model. With small models, retrieved labelled examples work better. Authors note generated examples can be invalid.
numbers: GSM8K: self-generated beats retrieved for text-davinci-003; retrieved stays ahead for smaller models; text-curie-001 about 2 to 3% in all methods.
limits: Table cell values partly garbled in extraction; direction of effect is stated in the text.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on self-generated analogs for weak models. Add a code check that the generated analog actually shows the claimed principle.

source: Franceschelli & Musolesi (2025) On the creativity of large language models
finding: Applies Boden's three types of creativity (combinational, exploratory, transformational) to LLMs. Argues current LLMs can reach at most combinational and exploratory creativity, and that transformational creativity is not reachable with present training.
numbers: Conceptual paper, no experiments. Boden criteria: new, surprising, valuable.
quote: Transformational creativity is not achievable through the current LLM training solutions.
limits: Opinion; RLHF is argued to reduce diversity (cites Kirk et al., 2024).
agent_relevance: Bounds what an O7/O6 scaffold can claim: recombination and exploration of the given space. Rule changes need a separate search and code checks (guardrail G8).

source: Boden (2004) The Creative Mind: Myths and Mechanisms, 2nd ed.
finding: From memory, not read this session. Creativity is producing ideas that are new, surprising and valuable relative to a conceptual space. Three forms: combinational, exploratory, transformational; P-creativity vs H-creativity.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened; the three criteria are confirmed only through the Franceschelli and Musolesi paper.
agent_relevance: Frames O6 as moving inside a space and O7 as combining across spaces.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction. Cognitive Science 13
finding: From memory, not read this session. ACME treats mapping as a connectionist constraint-satisfaction network over structural, semantic and pragmatic constraints.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. The lab PDF mirror returned nothing.
agent_relevance: A multi-constraint score (structure, meaning, goal) is a template for ranking candidate analogs in code.

source: Wikipedia Analogy, cognitive science section (read this session)
finding: Summarises Gentner's systematicity principle and Holyoak and Thagard's multiconstraint theory: structure, similarity, purpose. Notes Keane and Brayshaw's incremental model adds working-memory limits. Hummel and Holyoak (2005) recast it in a neural net.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia; only the first 100k characters were read.
agent_relevance: Confirms the three constraints we can encode as the mapping score: structure, similarity, goal fit.

source: Nersessian (2008) Creating Scientific Concepts
finding: From memory, not read this session. Argues scientists build and run mental models using analogy, visual imagery and thought experiments.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened; no open copy found. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Supports running a model as a simulation, which our code checker can do in place of a model opinion.

source: Hesse (1966) Models and Analogies in Science
finding: From memory, not read this session. Separates positive, negative and neutral analogy; neutral analogy is where new predictions come from.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Typed mapping with three bins: matched, known mismatches, open. The open bin lists testable predictions.
